case_study_insert.main_stem: Brightpath Dental Clinics (BDC) is a private limited company in the private dentistry sector, based in the Auckland region and running dental practices, employing a workforce of 40. Founded in 2017 by Dr Samuel Okafor, it receives referrals from local GP practices and operates a flat structure with democratic leadership. BDC plans to invest $520,000 in a new digital scanning and same-day crown unit with recyclable impression trays, financed by a $300,000 ten-year bank loan and $220,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $180,000 a year, a variable cost of $14 a unit and a selling price of $38, and produces 40,000 units a year. BDC faces a crown remake rate of 5.2% and dental nurse absenteeism of 10%.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Operations Log — Q4 2025: The clinic fitted 9,800 crowns last quarter at a remake rate of 5.2%, down from 7.0% a year earlier. Patient complaints fell from 33 to 19 a month. Average appointment waiting time is 9.5 days. A survey of 450 patients found 74% would pay $30 more for a same-day crown, and 63% choose clinics offering digital scanning. A skills audit shows 12 of 40 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new intraoral scanners; off-the-job training courses at the dental college cost $860 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Brightpath Dental Clinics for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Dental Sector Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.00%, increasing borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.4% from $13.90 to $14.79 per hour from April 2026, lifting dental-nurse payroll costs. (3) Impression material and scanning consumable costs have risen 8.9% year-on-year, while demand for same-day crowns grew 4.8%.

questions.question_text: BDC is funding part of its $520,000 digital scanning and crown unit with a $300,000 ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for BDC of using the $220,000 retained profit instead of borrowing more.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit has no interest charge or compulsory repayment, so BDC keeps the cash flow needed to meet fixed costs of $180,000 a year while it services the $300,000 loan. Every dollar not paid to the bank can absorb the 8.9% rise in impression-material costs, helping BDC hold its $38 selling price and keep same-day crowns competitive for the local GP practices that refer patients.

Point 2: Using $220,000 retained profit avoids more collateral and protects Dr Samuel Okafor's ownership. The $520,000 unit cannot be repossessed if demand falls short of the 40,000 units, and the survey finding that 74% of 450 patients would pay $30 more for a same-day crown gives BDC confidence to fund the launch from internal resources rather than add debt. With a 5.2% remake rate and 10% nurse absence already pushing up costs, keeping $220,000 free of interest gives room to fix problems without another bank payment due, and it avoids lender conditions on the $520,000 unit.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to BDC's financing decision and its dental operations.

questions.question_text: BDC is promoting its new same-day crown unit. Consider local radio advertising, partnerships with local GP practices, or social media campaigns. Which should BDC choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Local radio advertising: Radio can cheaply announce same-day crowns across the Auckland region and drive calls for appointments. It suits short, time-sensitive messages and is affordable for a 40-staff practice with a $300,000 loan. Its limit is that audio cannot show digital scanning or the 63% of patients who choose clinics offering it, and much of the audience may not need a crown, so wastage is high against the 9,800 crowns fitted last quarter.

Partnerships with local GP practices: BDC already receives GP referrals, so shared leaflets and practice visits would reach patients who need restorative work. This route is low-cost, credible and can highlight the 74% of 450 surveyed patients who would pay $30 more for a same-day crown and the 63% who want digital scanning. It builds more slowly than advertising and depends on GPs promoting one provider, but it fits BDC's flat structure, where clinicians can visit practices directly.

Social media campaigns: Targeted adverts can show scans and same-day results with measurable enquiries against the 9.5-day appointment waiting time. They are cheaper than radio per impression and reach younger patients, but dental decisions rely on trust and a click may not become a booked crown, so conversion is uncertain and the message competes with many clinics.

Recommendation: BDC should choose partnerships with local GP practices, supported by a small social media reminder campaign. This is the cheapest option, uses existing referrals and matches the 63% who want digital scanning. Radio is rejected as untargeted and unable to show the technology; social media alone is rejected because it lacks the clinical trust that a GP endorsement supplies for a $520,000 investment.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal application to BDC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of BDC with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of BDC with a well-justified recommendation explaining why radio and social media are rejected.

questions.question_text: BDC's crown remake rate is 5.2% and dental nurse absenteeism 10%. Explain two benefits for BDC of using democratic leadership with its workforce of 40.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership invites the 40 staff to suggest how the new intraoral scanners should be used, which suits BDC's flat structure and can push the 5.2% remake rate below last year's 7.0%. Clinicians who help set scanning routines are more likely to follow them, protecting the 9,800 crowns fitted last quarter and the $38 selling price.

Point 2: Being consulted raises job satisfaction and helps cut 10% nurse absence, because staff are more committed to attending when their views count. Better attendance shortens the 9.5-day appointment wait and reduces the need to retrain the 12 of 40 staff missing on-the-job training at $860 each, protecting the return on the $520,000 unit. In a flat structure clinicians are close to the patient and can see why a crown was remade, so their suggestions are practical and quickly applied; lower absence also protects the 9.5-day appointment wait that the 74% wanting a same-day crown care about, while the $860 college places can fund skills not learned chairside.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to BDC's remake rate, absence, training and expansion.

questions.question_text: BDC must train 12 of 40 staff who have not completed on-the-job training on the new intraoral scanners. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the dental college. Which should BDC choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching with the actual scanners is specific to BDC's crown workflow and costs no course fees, while the 12 trainees continue to support the 9,800 crowns fitted last quarter. Experienced clinicians can correct scanning technique at once, the quickest way to reduce the 5.2% remake rate below 7.0%. Drawbacks are that busy staff have less time to teach, shortcuts may spread, and there is no external certificate to show the 63% of patients who want digital scanning.

Off-the-job training: The dental college course at $860 per employee costs 12 × $860 = $10,320, small beside the $520,000 unit. It gives structured skills and a recognised certificate that supports the 63% who choose clinics offering digital scanning. However, it removes 12 of 40 staff from the practices, which could lengthen the 9.5-day appointment wait and worsen 10% absence, and generic teaching still needs adapting to BDC's scanners.

Decision: BDC should choose on-the-job training first, with a short certified college module later for lead clinicians. On-the-job coaching is cheaper, scanner-specific and avoids losing chairside capacity while absence is 10%. Full off-the-job training is rejected now because removing 12 of 40 staff would disrupt the 9,800-crown schedule and the $10,320 fee is premature before the 5.2% remake rate falls. With remakes at 5.2%, instant feedback on the actual scanner beats practising on examples that may not match BDC's cases. BDC should track the rate after a pilot and fund the $10,320 college route only if the remake rate fails to improve on the current 5.2%.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to BDC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of both training methods in the context of BDC.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and scanner relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how BDC's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $180,000 ÷ ($38 − $14) = $180,000 ÷ $24 = 7,500 units. Answer: break-even output is 7,500 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $38 − $14 = $24. Answer: contribution per unit is $24.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways BDC's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Comparing the 7,500-unit break-even output with actual output of 40,000 units gives a margin of safety of 32,500 units, showing how far crown demand could fall before the unit makes a loss.
2. Contribution per unit of $24 lets managers test pricing: a $2 discount from $38 to $36 leaves $22 contribution, so they can judge whether extra crowns still cover the $180,000 fixed costs.
3. Knowing fixed costs and contribution helps set the volume needed to service the $300,000 bank loan, checking the $520,000 unit can meet repayments.
4. Managers can benchmark unit cost, $180,000 ÷ 40,000 units = $4.50 plus $14 = $18.50 a crown, across quarters to spot the 5.2% remake rate and 10% nurse absence driving rework.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 7,500 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $24 | (iii) Four contextual uses: 32,500-unit safety margin against 40,000-unit output; discount pricing from $38 against $24 contribution; loan-service volume for the $300,000 borrowing; and unit-cost benchmarking at $18.50 to tackle remakes and absence.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate BDC's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has BDC's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 45.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 48.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 20.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 24.0%
ROCE 2024 = 16.0%
ROCE 2025 = 20.0%

Detailed workings: 2024 gross profit of $540,000 came from $1,200,000 revenue less $660,000 cost of sales, so $540,000 ÷ $1,200,000 × 100 = 45.0. In 2025, $1,500,000 revenue less $780,000 cost of sales gives $720,000, so $720,000 ÷ $1,500,000 × 100 = 48.0. Operating profit of $240,000 in 2024 and $360,000 in 2025 divided by revenue gives $240,000 ÷ $1,200,000 × 100 = 20.0 and $360,000 ÷ $1,500,000 × 100 = 24.0. Returns on capital were $240,000 ÷ $1,500,000 × 100 = 16.0 in 2024 and $360,000 ÷ $1,800,000 × 100 = 20.0 in 2025. Interest payable rose from $25,000 to $30,000, so the gain was not caused by cheaper borrowing.

Evaluation: Every measure improved. The gross margin rose from 45.0% to 48.0% because revenue grew from $1,200,000 to $1,500,000 while cost of sales increased less quickly, so each crown retained more after direct costs. The operating margin improved from 20.0% to 24.0%, showing the $180,000 fixed-cost base was covered much better as same-day crowns ramped up. Returns on capital climbed from 16.0% to 20.0% despite capital employed rising from $1,500,000 to $1,800,000, so the new unit is adding value. These are operational gains, since operating profit rose despite higher interest payable. The caution is the 5.2% remake rate and 10% nurse absence, which could lift costs or lengthen the 9.5-day appointment wait.

Conclusion: BDC's financial performance has improved. The gross margin (45.0% to 48.0%), operating margin (20.0% to 24.0%) and returns on capital (16.0% to 20.0%) all rose together on higher revenue and gross profit, not on accounting effects. BDC should protect the gain by cutting remakes and absence.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the three margins/return for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of revenue, costs, capital and interest movements and a justified conclusion on whether performance improved.

questions.question_text: BDC is considering offering recyclable impression trays across all its practices. Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for BDC of this decision.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Recyclable trays support the 63% of 450 surveyed patients who choose clinics offering digital scanning and help justify the $30 premium wanted by 74%, protecting the $24 contribution per crown on 40,000 units and the $520,000 unit investment.

Disadvantage: Recyclable materials cost more than standard trays, which would raise the $14 variable cost per unit unless the $30 premium is accepted on every crown. The insert gives no figure for the extra material cost, so the net effect cannot be quantified honestly. Any supply or sealing failure would also lift the 5.2% remake rate and lengthen the 9.5-day appointment wait before the new unit stabilises. Recyclable trays also reinforce the modern digital image that 63% of patients link with clinics offering scanning, supporting the $30 premium. No extra material cost is stated, so BDC should trial one practice and compare the 5.2% remake rate and complaint count before changing all 40,000 crowns.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to BDC's survey data, costs and quality record.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.00%, the 6.4% minimum wage increase to $14.79 and the 8.9% rise in impression material and scanning consumable costs will affect BDC. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.00%): The increase is 0.75 of a percentage point, so if BDC's $300,000 ten-year loan is variable-rate the extra cost is 0.75% × $300,000 = $2,250 a year (0.0075 × $300,000). That is modest beside fixed costs of $180,000, and a fixed-rate loan would avoid it entirely. Higher rates could make future borrowing for the $520,000 unit dearer and slightly dampen the 4.8% growth in demand for same-day crowns.

Minimum wage increase (6.4%, to $14.79 an hour): BDC's workforce of 40 includes hourly-paid dental nurses, so payroll costs rise and cannot be avoided. The insert gives neither hours worked nor individual pay, so an annual wage total would be invented. The defensible test is productivity: 40,000 units ÷ 40 staff = 1,000 crowns per worker, so the higher wage is affordable only if that rate holds or improves; cutting 10% absence and the 5.2% remake rate and training the 12 untrained staff can help sustain it.

Input cost inflation (8.9%): Impression materials and scanning consumables feed the $14 variable cost on every crown. The insert does not decompose that cost, so only a bound is honest: if the whole $14 were exposed, 8.9% × $14 = $1.246 per unit, and at 40,000 units that is 40,000 × $1.246 = $49,840 a year. Even a smaller exposed share would erode the $24 contribution on every crown sold.

Conclusion: The 8.9% rise in impression material and scanning consumable costs will have the greatest impact. It repeats across all 40,000 crowns and directly attacks the $24 contribution that services the $300,000 loan and funds the $520,000 unit, whereas the interest rise costs $2,250 a year and the wage effect can be offset by sustaining 1,000 crowns per worker. BDC should cut the 5.2% remake rate and seek the $30 premium rather than absorb the whole increase.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to BDC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on BDC's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in context with a well-justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.
